job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Victor Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied business information and finance at Corvale University and graduated in June. I live with my parents and my sister in a semi-detached house on Willow Lane. I wake up around seven, spend the morning writing Python scripts that pull financial data and build dashboards for my portfolio, then I apply to jobs and take calls with a couple of people in startups. In the evening I help my sister with her chemistry homework.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is that everyone wants three years of experience for a graduate job. I've applied to about seventy places and had six interviews, which isn't bad but isn't a job. What I still enjoy is the building: at my internship at a small payments startup called Fennel, I built a script that cut month-end reporting from two days to three hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a bubble, and some people should feel a bit silly. I'd say the useful bits, like code help and summarising, stay useful, and I'd keep using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my plan doesn't change much. I'd still be a graduate with some debt, about six weeks of savings, and the same job hunt. If AI is only mildly useful, it's still a good edge, since most of my competition doesn't use it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, and I'd lean into the startup scene where my script experience counts, like Fennel or similar. I'd send two or three really tailored applications a week instead of thirty generic ones. I'd keep building small tools and put them on my GitHub page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pretty fine. I'm a bit impatient, because I'm good at making things and bad at waiting, but I don't feel scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. If it turns out to be hype, what does that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make no difference to my daily routine, because the tools are already part of how I work. If it's hype, the market just stays the same speed, and I use my edge to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the weeks when nothing moves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the quiet weeks I'd build something. A script that scrapes job boards and ranks the ones that match my skills took me two evenings, and it got me two of my interviews.

say: I'd say it was **a bubble**, but the useful bits like code help stay useful.
I'd tell friends to keep using the tools that **save real time**.
think: My plan doesn't change much, and my **AI edge** helps because most competition ignores it.
I'm **good at making things** and bad at waiting.
do: Send **two or three tailored** applications a week, aimed at startups.
Keep building **small tools** and post them on my GitHub page.
Use my **job-board script** to rank openings that match my skills.
S0.quote: A script that scrapes job boards and ranks the ones that match my skills took me two evenings, and it got me two of my interviews.
fieldNote: Victor's mood is **uneasy rather than anxious**: skills, family help and six interviews give him control.
His reflex under pressure is to **build something**.
He is **impatient**, not fearful, which suits his adaptive profile.

steps.text: Send two or three tailored startup applications weekly
Publish small finance tools on my GitHub page
Run my job-board ranking script every morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the point where you either use the tools or fall behind. I'd say employers should train people, but nobody should wait for them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my plain reporting and reconciliation skills are going to be cheap, but a person who builds the workflows and checks them will be valuable. My worry is that firms decide they only want experienced people to do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd target roles in finance operations and fintech, where I can automate reports, and I'd learn one more tool each month, say a database plus an orchestration platform. I'd do a short certification in data engineering. I'd also invest 100 a month in a low-cost fund, to start owning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the best kind of nervous. I like change when I'm on the front side of it, though I know not everybody is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own skills are safe, and which aren't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plain spreadsheet reporting won't be safe. Safe is knowing what the numbers mean for a business and being able to explain it to a nervous manager. That's why I'm trying to talk to finance managers as well as coders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you will find this hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, honestly. He's a shift supervisor in a packaging plant, and he talks about it like it's something happening to other people. I'd have to talk him through it and he'll be stubborn.

say: I'd say you either **use the tools or** fall behind, and nobody should wait for employers.
I'd tell friends to **learn one new tool** each month.
think: Plain reporting skills will be **cheap**, but people who build and check the workflows will be valuable.
My worry is that firms want **only experienced people** for that.
do: Target **finance operations and fintech** roles where I can automate reports.
Do a short **data engineering certificate** and learn one tool each month.
**Invest 100 a month** in a low-cost fund to start owning something.
feel: It feels like the **best kind of nervous**, because I'm on the front side of the change.
S1.quote: Safe is knowing what the numbers mean for a business and being able to explain it to a nervous manager.
fieldNote: Victor treats disruption as an **advantage** but also sees firms asking for experience.
He plans **to own assets** with a monthly fund, an early sign of long-term thinking.
His concern for his **father** shows he cares beyond himself.

steps.text: Apply for finance operations and fintech roles
Complete a short data engineering certificate
Invest 100 monthly in a low-cost fund
Learn one new automation tool every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to need new rules quickly, and I'd say that without drama. Governments can't wait, and the companies building this should take part in the answer rather than hand over the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honestly nervous. If AI can do all thinking work by 2028, a graduate programmer-analyst is just one more thing it replaces. But I'd have a head start on most people and I'd use it as much as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small business in the first six months, something like AI reporting for small firms that can't afford it yet. I'd save every pound, and take any contract work to pay my way. I'd also learn a hands-on skill, like electrical work or kitchen fitting with my uncle, as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the starting gun went off early. I'm racing, but I'm not sure the track is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What is the first thing you do differently from your normal plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop sending applications to large firms, because they'd be shrinking, and I'd put all that time into the business. A paid contract would be worth more than ten applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do to avoid freezing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a list each Sunday: three things for the business, one for money, one for my body. When I'm busy I don't freeze, I just move and then think.

say: I'd say we need **new rules quickly**, with the companies building AI in the answer.
think: A graduate analyst is **one more thing it** replaces, but I'd have a head start.
I'm honestly **nervous** that the track might not be there.
do: Start my own **AI reporting service** for small firms in the first six months.
Take any **contract work** and save every pound.
Learn a **hands-on skill** with my uncle, like electrical work, as a hedge.
feel: It feels like the **starting gun went off** early, and I'm racing without a clear track.
S2.quote: I'd stop sending applications to large firms, because they'd be shrinking, and I'd put all that time into the business.
fieldNote: Victor's **adaptive style** turns fear into building, but his mood is still anxious: no income and a shrinking market.
He picks a **hands-on hedge** with his uncle, using the three-year robot gap.
His **Sunday list** shows how he keeps himself moving.

steps.text: Launch an AI reporting service for small firms
Take paid contract work and save every pound
Learn electrical work with my uncle as a hedge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal but one we can handle if we start now. I'd tell my friends to get a job in the middle of it all, not on the edge, so they can learn from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel decent. Five years gives me enough time to get a good first job at a company that's changing, build real skills and savings, and then start something. I'd feel worse if I were someone who refuses to touch the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first good job in fintech or finance operations and work hard for two years, saving 40 percent. Then I'd start a side project that turns into a business. I'd put the savings into index funds and keep learning the new tools every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a good test. I'd feel focused more than anything, and I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is your first year different when you have five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year would be about being inside, learning how a real company deploys AI, and being useful. With two years I'd skip that and build my own thing at once, but five years lets me learn on someone else's budget first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your sister and her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to learn chemistry for its own sake and to learn to write code on the side, because the combination is hard to replace. I'd offer to pay for her first course if she needs it.

say: I'd say it's a big deal we can handle if we **start now**.
I'd tell friends to get **inside a company** and learn from the inside.
think: Five years is enough for a **good first job**, real skills and savings, then my own thing.
I'd feel **worse** if I refused to touch the tools.
do: Take a **first fintech job** and save 40 percent for two years.
Start a **side project** that grows into a business.
Put savings into **index funds** and learn new tools every quarter.
feel: It feels like a **good test**, and I'd feel focused and sleep fine.
S3.quote: Five years lets me learn on someone else's budget first.
fieldNote: Victor's plan uses the extra time to **learn inside a firm** before founding anything.
He is **generous with family**, offering to help his sister with her first course.
His unease is low because **he sees a sequence** he can follow.

steps.text: Take the first fintech job and save 40 percent
Start a side project that could become a business
Put savings into index funds each month
Offer to pay for my sister's first coding course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and a chance to get things right. I'd tell my friends to enjoy it and build, and I'd tell the government to start training people for the new jobs now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm, honestly. Ten years is plenty to find a job, build something and save a good chunk. I'd even say it's a gift, because I can learn the tools while they're getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job, work my way up, and start a small business by 27. I'd keep learning, invest monthly and probably buy a small flat by 30. I'd stay curious about robotics too, since they arrive three years after the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting. I'd feel like I'm riding the front of a wave, and I'd enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, are you more relaxed or more ambitious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More ambitious, I think. With a decade I can try something, fail once and try again. That's a luxury that two years never gives anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good version of the next ten years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good version is a good job by next spring, my own project by 27, a flat by 30, and my parents proud and not worried. If I've got those, I'd be fine for whatever year ten brings.

say: I'd say it's a **long runway** and a chance to get things right.
I'd tell the government to **start training people** for the new jobs now.
think: Ten years is plenty to **find a job**, build something and save a good chunk.
I'd call it **a gift**, because I can learn the tools while they get better.
do: Get a **job and work up**, then start a small business by 27.
**Invest monthly** and aim for a small flat by 30.
Stay curious about **robotics**, since it arrives three years after the AI.
feel: It feels **exciting**, like riding the front of a wave.
S4.quote: With a decade I can try something, fail once and try again. That's a luxury that two years never gives anyone.
fieldNote: Victor's calm comes from **time, skill and small** safety nets, not from ignoring the risk.
He calls the decade a **gift**, a view only an adaptive person with family backing would hold.
He mentions **robotics** as the next step to watch.

steps.text: Take a first job and aim to move up
Start a small business by age 27
Invest monthly towards a flat by age 30
Keep learning each new AI and robotics tool

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too fast for a graduate to get a foothold and for the rules to arrive. What would help is a way to get paid while building a business, like a start-up grant for people under 25, and quick retraining paid by the companies that profit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not as sure as I sound. I tell myself I'm adaptive, but it's easy to be adaptive when you've got a family room to sleep in. I'd like to know what happens to people who don't have one.

headlineQuote: I tell myself I'm adaptive, but it's easy to be adaptive when you've got a family room to sleep in.
portrait: Victor is a 23-year-old **business information graduate** living with his parents and sister on Willow Lane, with seventy applications and six interviews.
He uses AI every day, writes **Python scripts** for his portfolio, and has some debt and six weeks of savings.
He is pragmatic and centrist, turns every worry into something to build, and is generous with his sister.
His mood runs from uneasy and anxious at two years to **calm at ten**, because he always has a plan.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, since graduates can't get a foothold and rules won't arrive in time.
whatWouldHelp: A **start-up grant** for under-25s and quick retraining paid by profiting firms would help.
